title: Training Curriculum: Lean Production for Team Leaders

content.text: Training Curriculum: Lean Production for Team Leaders
Programme owner: [PERSON_1], Head of Training and Development, [ORG_1]. Curriculum version 2.1, approved by the plant management on [DATE_1].

[ORG_1] manufactures hinges, drawer systems and fittings for the furniture industry at two plants, with around 1,250 employees in total. Over the past three years, we have introduced daily shop floor meetings, visual performance boards and a structured improvement process in all production areas. The experience so far is clear: lean methods only work in the long term if the team leaders on the shop floor understand them, use them every day and pass them on to their teams.

Team leaders are the link between plant management and the production teams. They organise the shift, solve problems, train new colleagues and are often the first to notice when a process is not running smoothly. However, most of our team leaders were promoted because of their technical skills and have never received systematic training in lean methods or in leading improvement work.

This curriculum describes a training programme of eight modules over six months that closes this gap. It combines short classroom units with practical work in the participants' own areas, so that every module produces a visible improvement on the shop floor. The programme was developed by the training department together with the production managers of both plants and the external lean consultancy [ORG_2], which also provides two of the trainers.

The programme is intended for team leaders and deputy team leaders in production, logistics and quality assurance at both plants. Shift supervisors who are about to take over a team leader role can also take part if their manager recommends them. Each run has 12 participants, so that there is enough time for individual coaching and for discussion of real problems.
Participants should meet the following prerequisites:
At least six months of experience as a team leader, deputy team leader or shift supervisor
Basic knowledge of the production processes and key figures of their own area
Basic computer skills, in particular working with spreadsheets
The agreement of their direct manager, who commits to supporting the improvement project described in section 11
No previous lean training is required. Participants who have already completed the internal one-day lean basics course can skip the first half of module 1 after consultation with the trainer.
After completing the programme, participants will be able to:
Explain the principles of lean production and the seven types of waste, and recognise waste in their own area.
Describe a value stream from goods receipt to dispatch and identify the main bottlenecks.
Organise their workplaces according to the 5S method and keep the standard stable over time.
Write, train and audit standard work instructions together with their teams.
Lead a daily shop floor meeting with visual performance boards and react to deviations in a structured way.
Solve problems systematically with the PDCA cycle, the 5-Why method and the A3 report.
Reduce changeover times with the SMED method.
Coach their team members to make and implement their own improvement suggestions.

The programme consists of eight modules. Each module starts with a classroom unit at the training centre of the main plant, followed by a practical assignment that participants complete in their own area within three to four weeks. At the start of the next module, each participant presents the results of their assignment to the group.
Problem solving with PDCA and A3
In total, the classroom part takes 9 days. In addition, participants should plan about four hours per week for their practical assignments, coaching sessions and the improvement project.

The first module introduces the basic ideas of lean production and shows why they matter for a company of our size. Participants learn how lean thinking developed, what the five lean principles mean in practice and how waste hides in everyday processes. A guided walk through the assembly hall of the main plant trains the eye for waste.
The five principles: value, value stream, flow, pull and perfection
The seven types of waste, with examples from our own plants
The role of the team leader in a lean organisation
Participants observe one workplace in their area for two hours and document at least ten examples of waste with photos and a short description.

In this module, participants learn to draw a current-state value stream map for a product family. They collect data such as cycle times, changeover times, inventory levels and lead times directly on the shop floor and calculate the share of value-adding time in the total lead time. On the second day, they develop a future-state map and derive concrete measures.
Selection of a product family and the customer demand rate
Symbols and data boxes of the value stream map
Calculation of lead time and the flow ratio
Design principles for the future state: flow, pull and levelling
Each participant maps the value stream of one product family in their area, in pairs if their areas are linked.

A clean and well-organised workplace is the basis for stable processes. Participants learn the five steps of the 5S method and how to make standards visible, so that deviations are recognised at a glance. The module puts particular emphasis on the fifth step, sustaining the standard, which is where most 5S initiatives fail.
Sort, set in order, shine, standardise and sustain
Shadow boards, floor markings and labelling
5S audits with a simple scoring sheet
Visual controls for materials, tools and machine condition
Participants carry out a complete 5S cycle at one workplace together with their team and introduce a monthly 5S audit.

Standard work describes the current best way to do a task. It is the basis for stable quality, for training new employees and for every further improvement. Participants learn how to break a task down into steps, key points and reasons, and how to train employees with the four-step method of job instruction.
Elements of standard work: takt time, work sequence and standard inventory
Writing work instructions with pictures and few words
Job instruction in four steps: prepare, present, try out and follow up
Training matrices to plan qualification in the team
Participants write or revise one standard work instruction, train two team members with it and update the training matrix of their team.

Daily shop floor meetings at the performance board are already in place in most areas, but their quality differs widely. In this module, participants learn how to lead a short, focused meeting, how to choose meaningful key figures and how to escalate problems to the next management level in a structured way.
Key figures for safety, quality, delivery and costs
Participants are observed by the trainer during two of their own shift meetings and receive written feedback.
Module 6: Problem Solving with PDCA and A3

Problems on the shop floor are often solved quickly but not permanently. This module teaches a structured approach that starts with a clear description of the problem and ends with a check of whether the measures were effective. Participants work on a real case from the plant during the classroom unit.
The PDCA cycle and its connection to the A3 report
Describing a problem with facts and figures
Root cause analysis with the fishbone diagram and the 5-Why method
Defining measures, responsibilities and an effectiveness check
Each participant solves one recurring problem from their area with an A3 report and presents it to their manager.

Short changeover times make it possible to produce smaller batches without losing capacity. In a simulation with a model press, participants experience how the time for a changeover can be cut in several rounds. They then analyse a real changeover in the stamping or injection moulding department with a video recording.
Quick-release fixtures, standardised tools and parallel work
Checklists and standard sequences for changeovers
Participants analyse one changeover in their area and implement at least three measures to shorten it.
Module 8: Leading Improvement and Final Presentations

The last module focuses on the team leader's role as a coach. Participants learn how to encourage employees to make suggestions, how to give feedback and how to keep the improvement process going after the programme. In the afternoon, each participant presents their improvement project to the plant management.
Coaching questions and the coaching kata
Handling suggestions in the company suggestion scheme
Personal action plan for the next twelve months

Each participant has 15 minutes to present the improvement project, followed by 10 minutes of questions from the plant management and the managers. The presentation follows the structure of the A3 report and shows the situation before the project, the root causes, the measures and the measured results. Participants are encouraged to bring members of their team who contributed to the project.

The programme follows the principle of learning by doing. Classroom units are kept short and interactive, and at least half of the time in each module is spent on exercises, simulations or work on the shop floor. The trainers use the following methods:
Short presentations with examples from our own plants and from other companies in the furniture supply industry
Group work on case studies and on the participants' own problems
Simulations, such as the model press in module 7 and a paper aeroplane production line in module 1
Guided observation on the shop floor
Individual coaching sessions between the modules, at least two per participant
All training materials, templates and recordings of the presentations are available on the
. Participants receive their login details one week before the start of the programme.

The programme is held in German, but all templates and handouts are also available in English, Polish and Turkish, because a significant number of our team leaders learned German as a second language. Trainers keep the language simple, explain technical terms when they are first used and give participants enough time for questions. Participants who would like additional support, for example with writing A3 reports, can book extra coaching hours with the training department. Shift workers who cannot attend a classroom day because of their shift pattern are released from their shift for that day, and their manager arranges a replacement in good time.
The success of the programme depends on several groups working together. The responsibilities are distributed as follows.

The trainers prepare and run the classroom units, review the practical assignments and hold the individual coaching sessions. Two trainers come from [ORG_2] and bring experience from lean projects in other manufacturing companies. The other two are experienced production engineers from our own plants who completed a train-the-trainer course in the previous year. Each module is run by one lead trainer, and a second trainer joins for the simulations and the work on the shop floor.

The direct managers nominate the participants, agree the improvement project with them and give them the time they need for the assignments. They attend the final presentation in module 8 and are responsible for the follow-up after the programme. Managers are invited to a two-hour briefing before each run so that they know what their team leaders will learn and how they can support them.

The training department organises the programme, books rooms and trainers, maintains the learning platform and keeps the qualification records. It also collects the feedback from participants and trainers and prepares the evaluation report for the plant management after each run.

The programme ends with an internal certificate that is recognised as a qualification for the team leader career path. To receive the certificate, participants must attend at least seven of the eight modules and pass the assessment, which consists of the following components:
documentation of at least six assignments
A3 report and presentation to plant management
Participants who do not pass a component can repeat it once, usually with the next run of the programme. The certificate is entered in the employee's qualification record in the HR system.

The programme runs twice a year, starting in March and in September. Classroom units take place from 7:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. in the training centre of the main plant, and the costs of travel from the second plant are covered by [ORG_1]. Lunch is provided. The time spent in the classroom and on assignments counts as working time.
To register, managers should send the following information to the training department at [EMAIL_1] at least six weeks before the start of a run:
Name and personnel number of the employee
A short description of the planned improvement project
Confirmation that the manager will attend the final presentation

If more than 12 registrations are received, the training department allocates places in consultation with the production managers, with priority for newly appointed team leaders. Questions about the programme can be directed to [PERSON_1] at [PHONE_1].
The costs of the programme are borne centrally by the training budget and are not charged to the cost centres of the participants. The budget for one run with 12 participants is planned as follows:

The working time of the participants is not included in this calculation. Based on the results of the pilot run, the programme pays for itself within the first year through the savings from the improvement projects.

Experience from other companies shows that much of what is learned in training is lost within a few weeks if it is not applied immediately. For this reason, each participant works on an improvement project in their own area throughout the programme. The project is agreed with the participant's manager before the start and should have a measurable target, for example a reduction of scrap, changeover time or search time.

The manager meets the participant at least once a month to discuss progress, removes obstacles and makes sure that the participant has the time to work on the project. Six months after the end of the programme, the training department carries out a short follow-up with each participant and their manager to check whether the new methods are still in use and whether the project results have been sustained.
Typical improvement projects from the pilot run included:
Search times for small parts reduced by 60 percent through a 5S cycle and a new kanban rack
New standard work instruction for the final inspection, which cut customer complaints in half
Changeover time on the 250-tonne press reduced from 74 to 31 minutes with SMED
Visual board for die condition, so that damaged dies are repaired before the next order
Fixed milk-run routes for the supply of the assembly lines, saving three forklift trips per shift

At the end of each module, participants rate the content, the trainer and the practical relevance on a short feedback form. After the programme, the training department evaluates the results together with the production managers and the trainers and adjusts the curriculum if necessary. The key figures for the success of the programme are the share of participants who receive the certificate, the results of the improvement projects and the scores of the 5S audits and shop floor meetings in the participants' areas twelve months after the programme.

The pilot run with 11 participants from the main plant ended last spring. Ten participants received the certificate, and the average rating of the modules was 4.4 out of 5. The participants rated the simulations and the practical assignments as the most useful parts of the programme, while several of them found the value stream mapping module too theoretical. For this reason, module 2 was extended by half a day of data collection on the shop floor, and the share of classroom presentations was reduced. The participants also asked for more time to exchange experiences with each other, which led to the introduction of a monthly team leader round table after the programme.
